So one question we've received at the launch of Common Assessments is who created these? Where do they come from? The first one is that these assessments were teacher created, either by using our approved materials and approved resources, H&H for elementary literacy as an example. The grade level and content expertise of teachers during our curriculum week over the summer, teachers worked on these to develop these. There's a group called VASCL, which is a consortium

of different school divisions that develop and share assessment materials aligned to SOLs. We're a member of that and we're able to utilize those and pull those into our Common Assessments as well. And so when we talk about Common Assessments, we are talking primarily here about using a tool called Performance Matters. So there are three different kinds of when we say assessments that are built into Performance Matters. The first one are Performance Matters short formatives. These are very short, maybe one assessment. That's what I was just referring to. Teacher teams creating these, aligning them, and continually evaluating them to make them better. And these are meant to be delivered at the end of a unit of

instruction, primarily. So these are meant to measure mastery after a time of instruction. And the third one is called Performance Matters Practice Comprehensives. These have been developed by Performance Matters aligned to our SOLs. These are longer assessments. They're more like a practice SOL, maybe something that a teacher might give once or twice a year towards the end of the year prior to an SOL to measure and practice student learning.

They're not required, but are available for teachers to use, as are the practice comprehensives. The LCPS Common Assessments were developed with principals and our level offices to think about what would be required and what would be optional. arts are required. And in three through five, science is required. K through two, science is optional. Social studies has a separate process around performance assessments that are part and tied to their the social studies equivalent of the standards of learning. So for example, if I'm going to hopefully explain this correctly, if there are multiple items measuring the same standard on an assessment, we would expect a student to do the same on those assessments, either to get those assessments correct or to get those questions incorrect. But if a student is getting one right and two wrong, that would be a sign that this might not be a reliable assessment.

So that's what's calculated through the coefficient alpha, and a 0.6 is considered a reliable assessment. You can see that this particular assessment is a 0.745, so we would consider this a reliable test. The next thing on here is the P value, and the P value is a measure of how hard or easy the questions are on the test. So a zero means it was really hard. A zero means nobody got it right. A one means everybody got it right. So somewhere in the middle tells us how hard or easy that test is.

This particular math assessment for fifth grade was a 0.63. And then below that is what you would call the P value sandwich. So what we're looking for when we're designing tests are to have some questions that are really challenging, some questions that are really easy, and a nice, healthy sandwich there in the middle.
